It occurred to me that the ownership of a sub would matter less if there was an effective way to move around a moderation issue. If I could type "general questions" and see all of the subs that qualified. Doing that requires tags, and resolving how tags get applied is complicated.

My idea is this: let users in a sub vote on what it is. Give them set of keywords to describe a sub, and let the users pick what they think they are there for. Not everyone will vote, but some will. Enough to guide the people that come after them. One tag per user per sub seems doable.

This lets multiple subs of a similar theme exist without stepping on each other. This lets users recover from a sub repurposed by nefarious means. If I can see where else to go, moderation skull-duggery is less useful, and therefore less likely.

First it's about survival. You get an axe, a pick, a sword, and some other basic supplies. You set out to chop down trees and build a shelter. In the day slimes bother you. At night, zombies and demons come out. It's recommended to have a structure of some kind to withstand the zombie attack each night.

As you dig and mine, you'll find ore that can be used to create tools, armor, and weapons. You'll also stumble across hidden caches of treasures. If you're lucky, you can find some pretty powerful items. The deeper you go, the more difficult it is to survive, but the better the treasures.

If you build multiple houses, people start showing up to live there. You can meet a merchant, a medic, and others.

It's really fun to play multiplayer but still really fun alone. Later in the game there are giant bosses that you can defeat and earn tons of loot.

As far as what kind of game it is, it's a 2D grid-based adventure/crafting game. Think Minecraft with one fewer dimension. The number of items in the game is insane. There are probably thousands of items. I know there are at the very least like 300 different tools and weapons.
What's really different between this game and something like Minecraft then? Apart from the fact that it's 2D rather than 3D ofc, as they just seem awfully similar to me :/

What's the difference between Tekken and Street Fighter II Turbo? What's the difference between Call of Duty and Halo? What's the difference between Mario Kart and Gran Turismo? Just because games are in the same genre, it doesn't mean they are alike.

Terraria is a lot more focused on verticality - gear upgrades, crafting, being able reach new depths and break into new biomes/areas. There's a very...not strict, but strongly recommended order you're intended to progress in, and often massive boss enemies serve as gatekeepers from one phase of the game to the next.

So, to me, Terraria feels more game-y than Minecraft does, but the sense of wonder and exploration isn't quite as strong in Terraria, aside from the initial novelty of finding things that were specifically added (new biomes, fun items, rare enemies). And of course constructing things in only two dimensions can be a bit stifling, creativity-wise.

From my understanding, aerobic exercise helps to stimulate myoglobin and hemoglobin generation. These are the oxygen carriers in muscle and blood respectively. In normal conditions (excluding scicle cell anemia and nutritional deficiencies) under aerobic stress, when the available oxygen is depleted, the body signals for more oxygen carrying proteins to be made. This means that the next time you exercise you have more oxygen available at the start of your exercise (bound to myoglobin in the muscle tissue) and a more efficient oxygen replacement system (more RBCs carrying more oxygen).
